source: v0 (Elzer/Carberry intended messages, FT Visual Vocabulary, Amar tasks) revised with taxonomy discovery on 500 panels (discovery_plot.json)

message.title: What the plot says
message.q: What should the reader conclude from this panel? One primary message, optionally one secondary. Decision rules: 4 or fewer compared entities = superiority gap, 5 or more = ranking; a reference from data or an oracle = fidelity-to-truth, from theory = prediction-match, from humans = agreement.

compare-superiority-gap.name: Ours beats baseline (gap)
compare-superiority-gap.def: One entity, usually the proposed method, is clearly better than one or a few baselines, and the size of the gap is the message.
compare-superiority-gap.include_if: There are two to four entities, one is highlighted, and the takeaway is 'X is better than Y by a margin'.
compare-superiority-gap.exclude_if: Use compare-ranking for a full ordering of many entities, and compare-consistency when the point is that the win repeats across facets or datasets.

compare-ranking.name: Ranking / leaderboard
compare-ranking.def: Many entities are ordered on a metric so the reader reads off the order, the top entity and the spread.
compare-ranking.include_if: There are five or more entities, or sorted bars or tables, and the reader cares about the full order or the top-k.
compare-ranking.exclude_if: Use compare-superiority-gap when only ours-versus-rest matters, and compare-consistency when the order is shown to repeat across settings.

compare-parity.name: Parity / on par
compare-parity.def: Two or more entities are shown to perform about the same, often to argue that a cheaper method loses nothing.
compare-parity.include_if: The curves or bars overlap, and the stated claim is 'comparable', 'on par' or 'no significant difference'.
compare-parity.exclude_if: Use robustness-insensitivity when the overlapping entities are settings of one knob rather than competing methods.

compare-consistency.name: Advantage holds across settings
compare-consistency.def: The same comparative result, such as ours being best or a fixed ordering, repeats across datasets, models, metrics or difficulty levels.
compare-consistency.include_if: The panel is faceted or grouped over settings, and the claim uses 'consistently', 'across all' or 'trends are consistent'.
compare-consistency.exclude_if: Use compare-superiority-gap when there is a single setting, and robustness-sensitivity when settings are levels of a perturbation and the point is how much the metric degrades.

compare-fidelity-to-truth.name: Estimate vs ground truth / exact reference
compare-fidelity-to-truth.def: Estimates from each method are plotted against a ground-truth, exact or oracle reference, either directly or as an error ratio, so the reader sees which method is closest.
compare-fidelity-to-truth.include_if: There is a truth, exact, oracle or reference-posterior curve, or the y-axis is error or ratio to the truth.
compare-fidelity-to-truth.exclude_if: Use theory-prediction-match when the reference is a theoretical prediction or fitted law rather than ground-truth data.

trend-monotone.name: Monotone / dose-response
trend-monotone.def: The metric rises or falls steadily with x, for example error growing with difficulty or task complexity.
trend-monotone.include_if: The claim is of the form 'more X gives more or less Y', with no special point on the curve.
trend-monotone.exclude_if: Use trend-scaling when the axes are log-log or compute/size with a power-law reading, and regime-failure-onset when there is a sharp cliff.

trend-scaling.name: Scaling law / cost growth
trend-scaling.def: A metric or cost is plotted against scale (nodes, compute, memory length, dimension), usually on log axes, to show its growth rate.
trend-scaling.include_if: The x-axis is a scale variable, log axes or power-law fits are used, and the claim is about the growth rate.
trend-scaling.exclude_if: Use regime-crossover when two scaling curves swap order and the swap point is the message.

trend-saturation.name: Saturation / diminishing returns
trend-saturation.def: Gains flatten as x grows, so extra budget, attempts or data stop helping.
trend-saturation.include_if: A plateau or shrinking increments is the stated point.
trend-saturation.exclude_if: Use tradeoff-budget-curve when cost and quality are plotted together to choose an operating point.

trend-training-dynamics.name: Training dynamics
trend-training-dynamics.def: Quantities are plotted over training steps or generations to show how a run behaves (stable, converging, co-moving metrics).
trend-training-dynamics.include_if: The x-axis is steps, epochs or generations, the point is the behaviour of the run itself, and there is no head-to-head method claim.
trend-training-dynamics.exclude_if: Use compare-superiority-gap when training curves are used mainly to show that ours ends above a baseline.

regime-crossover.name: Crossover / order flip
regime-crossover.def: Two or more curves swap their ordering at some x, so which option is best depends on the regime.
regime-crossover.include_if: The curves intersect and the claim is 'A is better below x*, B above'.
regime-crossover.exclude_if: Use compare-superiority-gap when one curve dominates everywhere.

regime-failure-onset.name: Collapse / cliff / divergence
regime-failure-onset.def: Performance breaks down sharply beyond a threshold or after some time (blow-up, cliff, collapse).
regime-failure-onset.include_if: There is an abrupt drop or explosion and the claim names a failure.
regime-failure-onset.exclude_if: Use characterize-failure-mode for a static breakdown of failure types with no threshold along x, and robustness-generalization-gap for seen-versus-unseen collapse.

regime-emergence.name: Emergence / step transition
regime-emergence.def: A property appears suddenly, as a step, jump or onset layer, instead of growing smoothly.
regime-emergence.include_if: There is a staircase or jump and the claim is 'emerges' or 'identifies at step k'.
regime-emergence.exclude_if: Use regime-failure-onset when the jump is a degradation.

regime-optimum.name: Interior optimum / U-curve
regime-optimum.def: A sweep has a best interior value, such as a U-shaped loss or a peak at r*.
regime-optimum.include_if: There is a U or inverted-U and the claim names an optimal setting.
regime-optimum.exclude_if: Use robustness-sensitivity when the sweep is shown to justify a hyperparameter range rather than to identify an optimum.

tradeoff-pareto.name: Pareto / frontier position
tradeoff-pareto.def: Methods are placed in a cost-versus-quality plane and ours sits on or beyond the frontier, in the 'good corner'.
tradeoff-pareto.include_if: It is a scatter or bubble of methods on two competing axes, and the claim is 'best of both' or 'Pareto-optimal'.
tradeoff-pareto.exclude_if: Use tradeoff-budget-curve when a single method is swept over a budget.

tradeoff-budget-curve.name: Quality vs budget curve
tradeoff-budget-curve.def: Quality is plotted against a swept budget (rate, max length, steps, sparsity), often with a paired cost panel, to show where a method sits.
tradeoff-budget-curve.include_if: The x-axis is a resource knob, and the claim is 'better quality at every budget' or 'flat until a knee'.
tradeoff-budget-curve.exclude_if: Use trend-saturation when no efficiency comparison is intended.

tradeoff-cost-advantage.name: Cost / overhead comparison
tradeoff-cost-advantage.def: Bars or lines show that ours uses far less compute or memory than a competitor, with no quality axis.
tradeoff-cost-advantage.include_if: Only the cost is shown and the claim is about efficiency.
tradeoff-cost-advantage.exclude_if: Use trend-scaling when growth with size is the emphasis.

attribute-ablation.name: Ablation (remove or swap component)
attribute-ablation.def: The full system is compared with variants that lack or replace a component, to show that the component matters.
attribute-ablation.include_if: Variants are named 'w/o X', 'LOO' or 'fix vs default', or are before/after a processing step.
attribute-ablation.exclude_if: Use attribute-intervention when there is a matched control and a dose knob.

attribute-intervention.name: Targeted intervention vs matched control
attribute-intervention.def: A specific internal component is amplified or removed, often at graded strength, against random or energy-matched controls to establish causal relevance.
attribute-intervention.include_if: There are control conditions, an α or γ strength axis, or removal from a mechanistic analysis.
attribute-intervention.exclude_if: Use attribute-ablation for an architecture or recipe component removed without a matched control.

attribute-decomposition.name: Decomposition into parts
attribute-decomposition.def: A total (runtime, score, competency profile) is split into components to show which part dominates.
attribute-decomposition.include_if: It shows stacked parts that sum to a whole, or a per-component profile of one total.
attribute-decomposition.exclude_if: Use characterize-failure-mode when the parts are error categories.

robustness-sensitivity.name: Sensitivity to perturbation or hyperparameter
robustness-sensitivity.def: The metric degrades or changes noticeably as a perturbation or hyperparameter varies.
robustness-sensitivity.include_if: It is a sweep, or a reference-versus-perturbed overlay, and the claim is 'degrades', 'depends on' or 'chosen setting'.
robustness-sensitivity.exclude_if: Use robustness-insensitivity when the claim is 'unchanged'.

robustness-insensitivity.name: Insensitivity / invariance
robustness-insensitivity.def: Results barely change across settings of a knob, so the method or conclusion is robust.
robustness-insensitivity.include_if: There are overlapping curves or bars across levels of one factor, with claims like 'remains comparable' or 'tracks the original'.
robustness-insensitivity.exclude_if: Use compare-parity when the overlapping entities are different methods.

robustness-variance.name: Variance / stability across runs
robustness-variance.def: Spread across seeds, checkpoints or test sets is the message (a tight method versus a noisy one, or an error margin).
robustness-variance.include_if: It is a strip, violin or replicate overlay, and the claim is about variance or stability.
robustness-variance.exclude_if: Use compare-superiority-gap when only means matter.

robustness-generalization-gap.name: Generalization / transfer gap
robustness-generalization-gap.def: Performance on seen or source conditions is contrasted with unseen or target conditions, often as a train-by-eval or source-by-target matrix with a strong diagonal.
robustness-generalization-gap.include_if: There are seen/unseen curves or a diagonal-dominant transfer heatmap.
robustness-generalization-gap.exclude_if: Use characterize-structure when the heatmap encodes similarity rather than transfer performance.

characterize-distribution.name: Distribution shape / shift
characterize-distribution.def: It shows a histogram, density or binned distribution of a quantity, or the overlap or shift between groups' distributions.
characterize-distribution.include_if: The form is a histogram, KDE, violin or binned shares, and the claim is about skew, modes, separation or overlap.
characterize-distribution.exclude_if: Use characterize-dataset-composition for descriptive benchmark statistics (sizes, shares) meant only to document the dataset.

characterize-structure.name: Latent structure / organization
characterize-structure.def: Clusters, blocks, spectra, subspaces or trajectories in a representation reveal an organizing structure.
characterize-structure.include_if: It is an embedding, block heatmap, eigen-spectrum, dendrogram or latent trajectory, and the claim is 'separable', 'block structure', 'outliers' or 'shared core'.
characterize-structure.exclude_if: Use association-agreement when the structure is explicitly matched against an external reference such as geography.

characterize-failure-mode.name: Failure-mode / error taxonomy
characterize-failure-mode.def: It shows which kinds of errors occur and how often, or which conditions models fail on.
characterize-failure-mode.include_if: There are error categories, confusion matrices, or condition-wise weakness bars (for example symbolic vs NL, naive vs non-naive).
characterize-failure-mode.exclude_if: Use regime-failure-onset when failure depends on a threshold along a continuous x.

characterize-dataset-composition.name: Dataset / benchmark composition
characterize-dataset-composition.def: Descriptive statistics document a new dataset or benchmark: shares, counts, coverage over time, lengths.
characterize-dataset-composition.include_if: It is a pie, donut, count bar or cumulative-growth plot in a dataset section, with no hypothesis tested.
characterize-dataset-composition.exclude_if: Use characterize-distribution when the distribution is evidence for a scientific claim.

association-correlation.name: Correlation
association-correlation.def: Scatter with a fit, or a correlation matrix, quantifying how strongly two measures move together.
association-correlation.include_if: It shows r or ρ, a fit line, or a correlation heatmap between metrics.
association-correlation.exclude_if: Use association-agreement when one side is a trusted reference that the other should reproduce.

association-agreement.name: Agreement with a reference / metric validity
association-agreement.def: A learned or automatic quantity is shown to match, or mis-match, a reference such as geography, human judgment or detector labels.
association-agreement.include_if: It shows split-triangle or overlay against a reference, a detector confusion matrix, or a metric-versus-perception check.
association-agreement.exclude_if: Use compare-fidelity-to-truth when several estimators compete to match the truth.

theory-prediction-match.name: Prediction / bound / fitted-law check
theory-prediction-match.def: Empirical points are overlaid on a theoretical curve, bound or extrapolated fit, and they agree.
theory-prediction-match.include_if: It shows theory lines with dots, fit-then-extrapolate, a bound above a measurement, or a tail-fit check of an assumption.
theory-prediction-match.exclude_if: Use theory-toy-illustration when there is no quantitative prediction, only a qualitative depiction.

theory-toy-illustration.name: Toy mechanism illustration
theory-toy-illustration.def: A constructed low-dimensional example (1-D function, quiver field, anchor embedding, smoothing sweep) makes a property such as continuity, an identifiability symmetry or convergence visible.
theory-toy-illustration.include_if: It uses synthetic or toy settings, and the claim is 'shows a jump', 'removes discontinuity' or 'converges to the mean'.
theory-toy-illustration.exclude_if: Use exemplify-qualitative-comparison when real-task outputs are being compared.

exemplify-qualitative-comparison.name: Qualitative side-by-side comparison
exemplify-qualitative-comparison.def: A grid of method-by-example outputs or overlays shows that ours looks better, or that the methods differ.
exemplify-qualitative-comparison.include_if: There are rows or columns of methods on the same inputs, with arrows, boxes or crops highlighting differences.
exemplify-qualitative-comparison.exclude_if: Use exemplify-illustration when only one method or the input data is shown.

exemplify-illustration.name: Illustrative example / schematic
exemplify-illustration.def: Representative inputs, outputs, environment renders, method pipelines or conceptual sketches orient the reader.
exemplify-illustration.include_if: It is a single-method example strip, a conceptual diagram, a case list, or a pipeline overview.
exemplify-illustration.exclude_if: Use exemplify-qualitative-comparison when two or more methods are contrasted.

modifier.title: Qualifier
modifier.q: How does the message qualify the comparison? Pick any that apply.

ours-better.name: Ours better
ours-better.def: the proposed method or condition comes out ahead

parity.name: Parity
parity.def: no meaningful difference, often a cheaper method matching a costly one

holds-across.name: Holds across settings
holds-across.def: the same result repeats across datasets, models, metrics or seeds

negative.name: Negative
negative.def: the plot shows something failing or not helping

vs-reference.name: Against a reference
vs-reference.def: compared with ground truth, an oracle, theory or humans

changes_from_v0: message labels rewritten from 500 annotated panels; added fidelity-to-truth, regime-optimum, cost-advantage, generalization-gap, dataset-composition, qualitative-comparison vs illustration
consistency and parity are also modifiers, not only messages (they qualify a comparison)
explicit decision rules for entity count and reference type, after annotators split identical panels between gap and ranking
